text.p: German chemical giant Hoechst AG said on Wednesday its 1997 net profit would turn out lower than in 1996, when the group reaped the benefits of extraordinary income from disposals.
However, the group said it still expected a slight rise in full-year operating profits on a comparable basis, when extraordinary gains from the sale of companies and shareholdings were stripped out.

"We are delighted that operating profit for the half-year came out where it did on a comparable basis, but the figures do need explanation," Klaus-Juergen Schmieder, Hoechst's chief financial officer, said in an interview with Reuters.
Shares in Hoechst were down 2.40 marks, around 2.8 percent, at 82.40 marks in late electronic trade, with the overall IBIS DAX index down 1.2 percent at the same time.
Operating profit fell 18 percent to 2.27 billion marks in the first half of 1997 from 2.775 billion marks in the same period last year, but rose on a comparable basis by seven percent.
Hoechst is one of Germany's big three chemical companies along with Bayer AG and BASF AG.
"If we can maintain the operating earnings growth of seven percent seen in the first half of the year, then we would be very happy," Schmieder said.
Christine Dienhart, chemicals analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich said: "Initially they said they were in line, but the more I look at them the more questions I have."

Ronald Koehler, chemicals analyst at BHF Bank: "I have some questions, but I think that ultimately these figures are above my expectations. I expect a move higher in the second half, especially given the favourable foreign exchange situation."

More than half of Hoechst's operating profit growth in the first half came from the strength of the dollar. "Over half of the seven percent growth in operating profit on a comparable basis came from the strength of the dollar," Schmieder said.

He said Hoechst had raised its forecast for the dollar/mark level for this year to 1.70 marks from 1.65 marks and that if the dollar stayed at its current high level then Hoechst would see stronger earnings growth in 1997.
"Naturally, however, other competitive conditions could change and dampen this effect," Schmieder said, admitting that Hoechst policy in this area was "cautious".
The dollar stood at around 1.84 marks on Wednesday.
"The currency situation is all very well as long as the dollar keeps rising strongly, but if the dollar starts to slow down, then what?" Dienhart said.
Sales at Hoechst in the first half were 27.886 billion marks compared to 26.091 billion in the same period of 1996.

In the first six months, sales in the group's pharmaceutical division were 7.091 billion marks, up from 6.438 billion marks. Of this, 7.038 billion marks was accounted for by the Hoechst Marion Roussel (HMR) unit.
Operating profit in the pharmaceuticals division fell to 1.054 billion marks from 1.159 billion marks. Operating profit at HMR was 1.002 billion marks, down from 1.051 billion.
"Looking at HMR, the trend seems to be toward lower operating margins, and it doesn't look like we're heading towards the 20 percent operating margin target," said Dienhart.
Its AgrEvo business, which it operates as a joint-venture with Schering, contributed 2.453 billion marks to sales, up from 2.258 billion marks.
Sales of specialty chemicals grew to 4.053 billion marks from 3.263 billion, Hoechst said.
Analysts had been expecting pretax profits of between 1.93 billion marks and 2.05 billion, with sales expected to come in between 26.35 billion marks and 27.2 billion.
